extracted.intended_audience: card issuers (larger and smaller), banks, credit unions, industry trade associations, consumer groups, compliance officers, and legal practitioners participating in CFPB rulemaking or implementing §1026.52 provisions
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and final-rule commentary on standards governing credit card penalty fees (especially late fees) under §1026.52, including safe-harbor amounts, annual CPI adjustments, special rules for charge cards, prohibitions, and the possibility of a courtesy period. Intended to guide issuers, commenters, and regulators on how fee reasonableness, proportionality, and adjustments will be evaluated and applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special rule for charge cards (§1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(C))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the special rule §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(C), a card issuer may impose a fee of 3 percent of the delinquent balance on a charge card account that requires payment of outstanding balances in full at the end of each billing cycle if the card issuer has not received the required payment for two or more consecutive billing cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This safe harbor provides charge card issuers more flexibility to charge higher late fees because charge cards do not apply an APR to the account balance and thus cannot increase a periodic rate in response to serious delinquencies. The final rule clarifies that issuers may impose such a fee notwithstanding the limitation on late-payment fee amounts in proposed §1026.52(b)(1)(ii). The CFPB declined to add an explicit textual limitation that the special rule applies only where there is no possibility of interest being charged because §1026.2(a)(15)(iii) already defines 'charge card' as an account where no periodic rate is used to compute a finance charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'charge card' (§1026.2(a)(15)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A charge card is defined as a credit card on an account for which no periodic rate (i.e., interest) is used to compute a finance charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of that definition, a credit card that charges interest on balances is not a charge card and therefore does not qualify for the special rule in §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(C), regardless of how a card issuer labels or markets the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve special-rule safe harbor amounts for charge-card issuers
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFPB determined not to lower the special-rule safe harbor amount for charge card issuers and is adopting proposed revisions clarifying fee imposition on seriously delinquent charge card accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB concluded preserving the special rule's current safe harbor amounts is necessary and appropriate to give charge card issuers flexibility to manage credit risk resulting from seriously delinquent accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual CPI adjustments for penalty fee safe-harbors (§1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(D))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(D) provides that the dollar safe-harbor amounts in §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(A) and (B) will be adjusted annually by the CFPB to reflect changes in the Consumer Price Index (CPI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB proposed to stop applying annual CPI adjustments to the late-fee safe harbor amount (by putting the $8 late-fee amount in the lead-in text) for Larger Card Issuers because CPI-based adjustments may not reflect issuers' actual costs and are not statutorily required. However, the CFPB retained the annual CPI adjustment for the safe-harbor amounts in (A) and (B) as they apply to Smaller Card Issuers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard: fees must be 'reasonable and proportional' (TILA §149)
rubrics_metrics.description: TILA section 149 requires that any late payment fee or any other penalty fee or charge must be 'reasonable and proportional' to the omission or violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In applying this standard, the CFPB considers costs incurred as a result of the violation (e.g., collection costs) and deterrence effects. The CFPB determined annual CPI adjustments were not necessarily reflective of issuer costs and thus may not align with the 'reasonable and proportional' requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of issuer costs when evaluating fee reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: Fee reasonableness should be evaluated by considering the costs incurred by card issuers as a result of the violation (e.g., collection costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB analyzed Y-14 collection cost data and preliminarily determined costs do not trend in lockstep with CPI; therefore, cost trends should be addressed via ad hoc adjustments rather than automatic CPI indexing. The CFPB will monitor data to inform adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of deterrence in fee-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Deterrence (the deterrent effect of the fee) is a factor the CFPB may consider when establishing safe-harbor amounts, but it should not outweigh considerations of issuers' costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB preliminarily determined it will not tightly peg deterrence to a specific value and recognizes a range of acceptable deterrent values. The CFPB also found deterrence does not move in lockstep with CPI and plans to consider deterrence alongside costs when making ad hoc adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ad hoc monitoring and adjustments instead of automatic CPI indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFPB's proposal and final decision favor monitoring the market and making ad hoc adjustments to safe-harbor amounts when warranted, rather than automatic annual CPI adjustments for Larger Card Issuers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB will monitor monthly per-account collection costs and CPI and will consider ad hoc revisions when market monitoring suggests a safe-harbor amount is no longer reasonable and proportional. The CFPB acknowledges monitoring obligations and will provide notice to issuers when adjustments are implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential treatment of Larger and Smaller Card Issuers
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule treats Larger Card Issuers and Smaller Card Issuers differently with respect to the late-fee safe-harbor amount and annual CPI adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Larger Card Issuers, the $8 late-fee safe-harbor amount is included in the lead-in text and annual CPI adjustments for late fees are eliminated; for Smaller Card Issuers the historical safe-harbor threshold amounts (e.g., $25/$35) and annual CPI adjustments in §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(D) are retained. The rule adds §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(E) to permit Smaller Card Issuers to impose late fees consistent with (A) or (B) notwithstanding the $8 limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific safe-harbor amounts for Smaller Card Issuers (comment 52(b)(1)(ii)-4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment 52(b)(1)(ii)-4 explains that, assuming historical safe-harbor thresholds, a Smaller Card Issuer may impose a late fee of $25 for a first late payment violation under §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(A) and $35 for a late payment violation that occurs during the same billing cycle or one of the next six billing cycles under §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(B), provided consistency with §1026.52(b)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comment is adopted to facilitate compliance by Smaller Card Issuers; those amounts remain subject to annual CPI adjustments under §1026.52(b)(1)(ii)(D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited fees (§1026.52(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1026.52(b)(2) prohibits (1) fees that exceed the dollar amount associated with the violation; and (2) multiple fees based on a single event or transaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A card issuer must not impose a fee for violating the terms of an open-end (non home-secured) consumer credit plan unless the dollar amount of the fee is consistent with §1026.52(b)(1) and (2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of a 15-day courtesy period
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFPB solicited comments on whether §1026.52(b)(2) should be amended to provide a 15-calendar-day courtesy period after each payment due date during which late fees could not be imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale for a courtesy period included that issuers may not incur significant collection costs immediately after a due date, processing delays can cause late payments, and consumer-conduct considerations (e.g., attempted timely payment). The CFPB asked whether such a courtesy period should apply only when using the safe-harbor or generally, and whether a shorter or longer period would be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of unintended consequences of a courtesy period
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFPB evaluated how a 15-day courtesy period could interact with safe-harbor usage and cost-analysis fee-setting, potentially producing perverse incentives or differential recovery outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Y-14 data, the CFPB estimated a 15-day courtesy period could cut the incidence of the proposed $8 safe-harbor late fee by as much as half, potentially causing issuers using the safe harbor to recover less per late-payment than issuers using the cost-analysis approach who might charge lower fees more frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of stakeholder comments on the courtesy period
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFPB considered supportive and opposing comments: supporters (consumer groups, some credit unions) argued a 15-day courtesy period would prevent abuses and align with industry practice; opponents (banks, credit unions, trade associations) argued existing 21-day statement timing functions similarly, a courtesy period could conflict with statutory ability to treat payments as late immediately, and it could confuse consumers or harm credit outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB weighed these arguments in deciding whether and how to implement any courtesy-period requirement and considered potential consumer confusion (e.g., due-date vs. late-fee date, impact on credit scores) and operational implications for issuers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of other penalty fees regarding CPI adjustments and courtesy periods
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFPB solicited comments on whether elimination of annual CPI adjustments or implementation of a courtesy period should apply to other penalty fees subject to §1026.52(b) (e.g., over-the-limit fees, returned-payment fees, declined access check fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB declined to apply the elimination of annual adjustments to all other credit card penalty fees at this time because it did not have the same in-depth data for those fees as it did for late fees; it solicited data and comment on appropriate monitoring or adjustment mechanisms for those fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that ad hoc adjustments provide notice and conform to CFPB monitoring obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the CFPB makes ad hoc adjustments to safe-harbor amounts, such adjustments must be implemented in a way that provides notice to card issuers, consistent with the CFPB's monitoring and reporting obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB acknowledged commenters concerned that manual monitoring and ad hoc adjustments could be burdensome but noted the CFPB is obligated to monitor and report on the credit card market and would provide notice when adjustments are made.
